claim: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) represent a substantial fraction of the Pol II transcripts in multicellular animals.
source: Though long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) represent a substantial fraction of the Pol II transcripts in multicellular animals, only a few have known functions.
evidence: This is a general statement about lncRNAs in the field, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Only a few lncRNAs have known functions.
source: Though long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) represent a substantial fraction of the Pol II transcripts in multicellular animals, only a few have known functions.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The blocking activity of the Bithorax complex (BX-C) Fub-1 boundary is segmentally regulated by its own lncRNA.
source: Here we report that the blocking activity of the Bithorax complex (BX-C) Fub-1 boundary is segmentally regulated by its own lncRNA.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The Fub-1 boundary is located between the Ultrabithorax (Ubx) gene and the bxd/pbx regulatory domain.
source: The Fub-1 boundary is located between the Ultrabithorax (Ubx) gene and the bxd/pbx regulatory domain, which is responsible for regulating Ubx expression in parasegment PS6/segment A1.
evidence: This is a description of the genomic location of Fub-1, supported by the genomic maps shown in the figures.

claim: The bxd/pbx regulatory domain is responsible for regulating Ubx expression in parasegment PS6/segment A1.
source: The Fub-1 boundary is located between the Ultrabithorax (Ubx) gene and the bxd/pbx regulatory domain, which is responsible for regulating Ubx expression in parasegment PS6/segment A1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the BX-C regulatory architecture.

claim: Fub-1 consists of two hypersensitive sites, HS1 and HS2.
source: Fub-1 consists of two hypersensitive sites, HS1 and HS2.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data and molecular characterization presented in the manuscript.

claim: HS1 is an insulator.
source: HS1 is an insulator while HS2 functions primarily as an lncRNA promoter.
evidence: This is supported by functional assays showing HS1 blocks crosstalk in replacement experiments.

claim: HS2 functions primarily as an lncRNA promoter.
source: HS1 is an insulator while HS2 functions primarily as an lncRNA promoter.
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data showing transcription from HS2 and the presence of promoter elements.

claim: To activate Ubx expression in PS6/A1, enhancers in the bxd/pbx domain must be able to bypass Fub-1 blocking activity.
source: To activate Ubx expression in PS6/A1, enhancers in the bxd/pbx domain must be able to bypass Fub-1 blocking activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the genomic organization and the requirement for enhancer-promoter communication.

claim: The expression of the Fub-1 lncRNAs in PS6/A1 from the HS2 promoter inactivates Fub-1 insulating activity.
source: We show that the expression of the Fub-1 lncRNAs in PS6/A1 from the HS2 promoter inactivates Fub-1 insulating activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from replacement experiments and smFISH showing correlation between lncRNA expression and loss of blocking.

claim: Inactivation of Fub-1 is due to read-through as the HS2 promoter must be directed toward HS1 to disrupt blocking.
source: Inactivation is due to read-through as the HS2 promoter must be directed toward HS1 to disrupt blocking.
evidence: This is supported by orientation-dependent effects in replacement experiments and rescue by transcription terminators.

claim: The vast majority of Pol II transcripts encoded by the genomes of multicellular animals correspond to long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), not mRNAs.
source: The vast majority of Pol II transcripts encoded by the genomes of multicellular animals correspond to long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), not mRNAs.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of genomics.

claim: The wide distribution of lncRNAs in the genome and the fact that their expression is often coordinated with genes in the immediate vicinity have led to the idea that they have functions in gene regulation and chromosome organization.
source: Their wide distribution in the genome and the fact that their expression is often coordinated with genes in the immediate vicinity have led to the idea that they have functions in gene regulation and chromosome organization (Herman et al., 2022; Li and Fu, 2019; Núñez-Martínez and Recillas-Targa, 2022; Statello et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles in the field.

claim: The primary sequences of lncRNAs are usually not very well conserved across species, unlike the sequences of protein coding mRNAs.
source: Unlike the sequences of protein coding mRNAs, which are typically conserved across species, the primary sequences of lncRNAs are usually not very well conserved.
evidence: This is established knowledge about lncRNA evolution.

claim: Some lncRNAs contain short sequence blocks that exhibit a relatively high degree of conservation, even though most of the lncRNA are divergent.
source: However, some lncRNAs contain short sequence blocks that exhibit a relatively high degree of conservation, even though most of the lncRNA are divergent.
evidence: This is established knowledge about lncRNA evolution and structure.

claim: Xist is a mammalian X chromosome inactivation lncRNA.
source: A classic example is the mammalian X chromosome inactivation lncRNA Xist.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Xist function.

claim: Conserved RNA sequence blocks within the Xist transcript function in recruiting Polycomb (PcG) silencing factors and targeting the transcript to the X chromosome.
source: Conserved RNA sequence blocks within the Xist transcript function in recruiting Polycomb (PcG) silencing factors and targeting the transcript to the X chromosome (Jacobson et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2020; Pandya-Jones et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Xist function.

claim: The HoxA complex lncRNA HOTT1P encodes RNA sequences that recruit chromatin modifiers that help promote gene expression.
source: Other lncRNAs, like the HoxA complex lncRNA HOTT1P, encode RNA sequences that recruit chromatin modifiers that help promote gene expression (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on HOTT1P.

claim: In some cases, the lncRNA itself does not appear to have important functions, but instead it is the regulatory elements (enhancers, silencers, and promoters) that control the expression of the lncRNA that are functionally important.
source: In other cases, the lncRNA itself does not appear to have important functions. Instead, it is the regulatory elements (enhancers, silencers, and promoters) that control the expression of the lncRNA that are functionally important (Ibragimov et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The expression of the Myc gene is downregulated by a mechanism in which the promoter for the PVT1 lncRNA competes with Myc for physical interactions with a set of shared enhancers.
source: For example, the expression of the Myc gene is downregulated by a mechanism in which the promoter for the PVT1 lncRNA competes with Myc for physical interactions with a set of shared enhancers.
evidence: This is an example cited from the literature about lncRNA regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Transcription of the ThymoD lncRNA helps regulate the expression of Bcl11b, a gene that plays an important role in specifying T cell fate.
source: Isoda et al. found that transcription of ThymoD lncRNA helps regulate the expression of Bcl11b, a gene that plays an important role in specifying T cell fate (Isoda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study by Isoda et al.

claim: Transcription of the ThymoD lncRNA induces the demethylation of recognition sites for the chromosomal architectural protein CTCF, enabling CTCF to bind to these sites and induce looping between the Bcl11b enhancers and the Bcl11b gene.
source: Transcription of the lncRNA induces the demethylation of recognition sites for the chromosomal architectural protein CTCF, enabling CTCF to bind to these sites and induce looping between the Bcl11b enhancers and the Bcl11b gene.
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Isoda et al., 2017.

claim: Ubx, together with abdominal-A (abd-a) and Abdominal-B (Abd-B), are responsible for specifying the identity of the nine parasegments (PS)/segments that form the posterior two-thirds of the fly.
source: Ubx, together with abdominal-A (abd-a) and Abdominal-B (Abd-B), are responsible for specifying the identity of the nine parasegments (PS)/segments that form the posterior two-thirds of the fly (Maeda and Karch, 2015: Figure 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about BX-C function, supported by a citation and Figure 1.

claim: Ubx is responsible for specifying parasegments PS5 (adult cuticle segment T3) and PS6 (adult cuticle segment A1).
source: Ubx is responsible for specifying parasegments PS5 (adult cuticle segment T3) and PS6 (adult cuticle segment A1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ubx function in BX-C.

claim: Ubx expression in PS5 and PS6 is controlled by the abx/bx and bxd/pbx regulatory domains, respectively.
source: Its expression in these two parasegments is controlled by the abx/bx and bxd/pbx regulatory domains, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BX-C regulatory architecture.

claim: abd-A expression in PS7-PS9 is directed by the iab-2–iab-4 regulatory domains.
source: abd-A expression in PS7-PS9 is directed by the iab-2–iab-4 regulatory domains, while Abd-B expression in PS10-14 is regulated by the iab-5–iab-9 regulatory domains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BX-C regulatory architecture.

claim: Abd-B expression in PS10-14 is regulated by the iab-5–iab-9 regulatory domains.
source: abd-A expression in PS7-PS9 is directed by the iab-2–iab-4 regulatory domains, while Abd-B expression in PS10-14 is regulated by the iab-5–iab-9 regulatory domains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BX-C regulatory architecture.

claim: Each BX-C regulatory domain has an initiation element, a set of tissue-specific enhancers, and Polycomb Response Elements (PREs).
source: Each regulatory domain has an initiation element, a set of tissue-specific enhancers, and Polycomb Response Elements (PREs) (Iampietro et al., 2010; Maeda and Karch, 2015; Maeda and Karch, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about BX-C regulatory architecture, supported by citations.

claim: Early in development, a combination of maternal, gap, and pair-rule gene proteins interact with the initiation elements in each regulatory domain, and set the domain in either the 'off' or 'on' state.
source: Early in development, a combination of maternal, gap, and pair-rule gene proteins interact with the initiation elements in each regulatory domain, and set the domain in either the 'off' or 'on' state.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BX-C regulation during development.

claim: The BX-C regulatory domains are sequentially activated along the anterior–posterior axis of the embryo.
source: The BX-C regulatory domains are sequentially activated along the anterior–posterior axis of the embryo.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BX-C regulation.

claim: In PS5(T3) only the abx/bx domain is activated and it is responsible for regulating Ubx expression in this parasegment.
source: For example, in PS5(T3) only the abx/bx domain is activated (all of the remaining BX-C domains including bxd/pbx are 'off') and it is responsible for regulating Ubx expression in this parasegment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BX-C regulation in PS5.

claim: Both abx/bx and bxd/pbx are turned on in PS6(A1); however, Ubx expression and parasegment identity depend on the bxd/pbx domain.
source: Both abx/bx and bxd/pbx are turned on in PS6(A1); however, Ubx expression and parasegment identity depend on the bxd/pbx domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BX-C regulation in PS6.

claim: Once the activity state of the domain is set in early embryos, it is remembered during the remainder of development by the action of Polycomb Group proteins (PcG: off) and Trithorax group proteins (Trx: on).
source: Once the activity state of the domain is set in early embryos, it is remembered during the remainder of development by the action of Polycomb Group proteins (PcG: off) and Trithorax group proteins (Trx: on).
evidence: This is established knowledge about epigenetic memory in BX-C.

claim: Each BX-C domain contains tissue- and stage-specific enhancers that drive the expression of its target homeotic gene in a pattern appropriate for proper development of the parasegment it specifies.
source: Each domain also contains tissue- and stage-specific enhancers that drive the expression of its target homeotic gene in a pattern appropriate for proper development of the parasegment it specifies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BX-C enhancer function.

claim: The Drosophila melanogaster Bithorax complex (BX-C) contains the Hox genes Ubx, abd-A, and Abd-B.
source: The Drosophila melanogaster Bithorax complex (BX-C), which contains the Hox genes Ubx, abd-A, and Abd-B, is shown in relation to where these three genes are expressed in an embryo.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and is established knowledge.

claim: There are nine cis-regulatory domains that are responsible for the regulation of Ubx (abx/bx and bxd/pbx domains), abd-A (iab-2–4 domains), and Abd-B (iab-5–7 and iab-8,9 domains), and for the development of parasegments 5–13 (PS)/segments (T3–A8).
source: There are nine cis-regulatory domains that are responsible for the regulation of Ubx (abx/bx and bxd/pbx domains), abd-A (iab-2–4 domains), and Abd-B (iab-5–7 and iab-8,9 domains), and for the development of parasegments 5–13 (PS)/segments (T3–A8).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and is established knowledge about BX-C organization.

claim: Fub-1 is bound by the chromosomal architectural proteins CTCF, CP190, Zw5, Pita, and Elba in ChIP experiments.
source: In ChIP experiments, Fub-1 is bound by the chromosomal architectural proteins CTCF, CP190, Zw5, Pita, and Elba and marks the border of a Polycomb histone H3K27me3 domain in PS5/T3 cells (Bowman et al., 2014, p. 27; Fuda et al., 2015; Harrison et al., 2011; Ueberschär et al., 2019; Zolotarev et al., 2016; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to ChIP-seq studies and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fub-1 marks the border of a Polycomb histone H3K27me3 domain in PS5/T3 cells.
source: In ChIP experiments, Fub-1 is bound by the chromosomal architectural proteins CTCF, CP190, Zw5, Pita, and Elba and marks the border of a Polycomb histone H3K27me3 domain in PS5/T3 cells (Bowman et al., 2014, p. 27; Fuda et al., 2015; Harrison et al., 2011; Ueberschär et al., 2019; Zolotarev et al., 2016; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to ChIP-seq studies and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNA Pol II and the histone mark for active transcription, H3K4me3, both map to Fub-1.
source: In addition, RNA Pol II and the histone mark for active transcription, H3K4me3, both map to Fub-1.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The signal for H3K4me3 in PS7 cell ChIPs is greater than that observed in mixed ChIPs.
source: Consistent with the results described below, the signal for H3K4me3 in PS7 cell ChIPs is greater than that observed in mixed ChIPs (Bowman et al., 2014, p. 27).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to ChIP-seq data.

claim: There are two prominent Zelda peaks and a putative enhancer located between Fub-1 and the Ubx promoter.
source: In between Fub-1 and the Ubx promoter, there are two prominent Zelda peaks and a putative enhancer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Harrison et al., 2011).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and supported by a citation.

claim: The bxd/pbx domain controls the expression of two lncRNAs, bxd and Fub-1 HS2.
source: Besides directing the expression of Ubx in PS6(A1) and more posterior parasegements, the bxd/pbx domain also controls the expression of two lncRNAs, bxd and Fub-1 HS2, Fub-1HS2.
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data and previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The bxd lncRNA initiates from a promoter close to the pbx enhancer and extends into the region located in between Fub-1 and the Ubx promoter.
source: Pease et al. found that the bxd lncRNA initiates from a promoter close to the pbx enhancer and extends into the region located in between Fub-1 and the Ubx promoter (Pease et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pease et al., 2013.

claim: The bxd lncRNA is first detected at the blastoderm stage as a broad band that extends from PS6/A1 to PS12/A7.
source: The bxd lncRNA is first detected at the blastoderm stage as a broad band that extends from PS6/A1 to PS12/A7.
evidence: This is based on the findings of Pease et al., 2013.

claim: Between the onset of gastrulation and stage 10, bxd lncRNA expression resolves into a series of eight stripes of differing intensity that span PS6/A1–PS12/A7.
source: Between the onset of gastrulation and stage 10 bxd lncRNA expression resolves into a series of eight stripes of differing intensity that span PS6/A1–PS12/A7.
evidence: This is based on the findings of Pease et al., 2013.

claim: Pease et al. detected a second bxd/pbx-dependent lncRNA, Fub-1HS2, which is expressed in PS6 (A1) and more posterior parasegments.
source: Pease et al. also detected a second bxd/pbx-dependent lncRNA, Fub-1HS2. Like bxd lncRNA, it is expressed in PS6 (A1) and more posterior parasegments.
evidence: This is based on the findings of Pease et al., 2013.

claim: The Fub-1HS2 lncRNA is encoded by sequences located between Ubx and Fub-1, including sequences in Fub-1 HS1.
source: This lncRNA is encoded by sequences located between Ubx and Fub-1, including sequences in Fub-1 HS1, and based on the in situ experiments of Pease et al., it likely originates from Fub-1 HS2.
evidence: This is inferred from the in situ experiments of Pease et al.

claim: Fub-1HS2 shares exon sequences with the bxd lncRNA.
source: Fub-1HS2 shares exon sequences with the bxd lncRNA.
evidence: This is based on the findings of Pease et al., 2013.

claim: The Fub-1HS2 lncRNA is detected in PS6/A1 and more posterior segments after the bxd lncRNA disappears.
source: However, the Fub-1HS2 lncRNA is detected in PS6/A1 and more posterior segments after the bxd lncRNA disappears.
evidence: This is based on the findings of Pease et al., 2013.

claim: The Fub-1 hypersensitive sites are evolutionarily conserved.
source: As has been reported for the regulatory elements associated with other lncRNAs, the Fub-1 hypersensitive sites are evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Key sequence blocks within HS1 and HS2 are detected not only in other members of the Sophophora subgenus, but also in Drosophila virilis, a distantly related member of the Drosophila subgenus.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2, key sequence blocks within HS1 and HS2 are detected not only in other members of the Sophophora subgenus, but also in Drosophila virilis, a distantly related member of the Drosophila subgenus.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The conserved blocks in HS1 include the dCTCF recognition site.
source: The conserved blocks in HS1 include the dCTCF recognition site, while in HS2 the conserved blocks include several GAGA motifs that correspond to binding sites for the GAGA factor (GAF) as well as the predicted transcription start sites for the Fub-1HS2 lncRNA.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The conserved blocks in HS2 include several GAGA motifs that correspond to binding sites for the GAGA factor (GAF) as well as the predicted transcription start sites for the Fub-1HS2 lncRNA.
source: The conserved blocks in HS1 include the dCTCF recognition site, while in HS2 the conserved blocks include several GAGA motifs that correspond to binding sites for the GAGA factor (GAF) as well as the predicted transcription start sites for the Fub-1HS2 lncRNA.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fub-1 and Fub define a TAD that encompasses the bxd/pbx regulatory domain and the Ubx transcription unit.
source: As shown in Figure 2, both regulatory domains (plus the Ubx transcription unit) are encompassed in a large TAD that extends from Fub-2 on the centromere proximal side of Ubx to Fub on the distal side.
evidence: This is shown in the Micro-C contact maps in Figure 2.

claim: Within the large TAD encompassing bxd/pbx and Ubx, there is an ~50 kb sub-TAD that spans bxd/pbx and is delimited by Fub-1 on the left and Fub on the right.
source: Within this large TAD, there is an ~50 kb sub-TAD that spans bxd/pbx and is delimited by Fub-1 on the left and Fub on the right (Figure 2B and C, black arrow).
evidence: This is shown in the Micro-C contact maps in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The bxd/pbx sub-TAD includes several smaller chromosomal segments that exhibit a high density of internal contacts (HDICs).
source: This bxd/pbx sub-TAD includes several smaller chromosomal segments that exhibit a high density of internal contacts (HDICs).
evidence: This is shown in the Micro-C contact maps in Figure 2.

claim: The endpoint for one HDIC domain maps to Fub-1, while the other endpoint maps to the bxd PRE.
source: The endpoint for one of these HDIC domains maps to Fub-1, while the other endpoint maps to the bxd PRE.
evidence: This is shown in the Micro-C contact maps in Figure 2.

claim: There is a second HDIC domain linking Fub-1 to sequences just upstream of the Ubx promoter.
source: There is a second HDIC domain linking Fub-1 to sequences just upstream of the Ubx promoter.
evidence: This is shown in the Micro-C contact maps in Figure 2.

claim: The Ubx promoter is linked to the bxd PRE by a lower density of internal contacts domain (LDIC) that is marked at the apex by an interaction dot.
source: The Ubx promoter is also linked to the bxd PRE by a lower density of internal contacts domain (LDIC) that is marked at the apex by an interaction dot (*).
evidence: This is shown in the Micro-C contact maps in Figure 2.

claim: The bxd PRE forms an interaction dot with the bx PRE.
source: The bxd PRE also forms an interaction dot (>) with the bx PRE as does the Ubx promoter (x).
evidence: This is shown in the Micro-C contact maps in Figure 2.

claim: The Ubx promoter forms an interaction dot with the bx PRE.
source: The bxd PRE also forms an interaction dot (>) with the bx PRE as does the Ubx promoter (x).
evidence: This is shown in the Micro-C contact maps in Figure 2.

claim: PREs in other developmental loci have been shown to interact with each other and also function as 'tethering' elements helping to link distant enhancers to their target genes.
source: Interestingly PREs in other developmental loci have recently been shown to interact with each other and also function as 'tethering' elements helping to link distant enhancers to their target genes (Batut et al., 2022; Eagen et al., 2017; Ibragimov et al., 2022; Levo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies on PRE function.

claim: F1attP flies do not show any evidence of a GOF transformation and their morphology is indistinguishable from wild type.
source: Unexpectedly, however, F1attP flies do not show any evidence of a GOF transformation and their morphology is indistinguishable from wild type (WT) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A comparing adult cuticle morphology.

claim: The sub-TAD linking Fub-1 to Fub that encompassed the bxd/pbx regulatory domain disappears in the Fub-1 deletion.
source: Figure 2B and C show that the sub-TAD linking Fub-1 to Fub that encompassed the bxd/pbx regulatory domain disappears in the Fub-1 deletion.
evidence: This is shown in the Micro-C contact maps in Figure 2B and C.

claim: In the Fub-1 deletion, the element located just upstream of the Ubx promoter forms a sub-TAD domain with the bxd PRE.
source: Instead, the element located just upstream of the Ubx promoter forms a sub-TAD domain with the bxd PRE (see interaction dot in Figure 2B and C [*] at the apex).
evidence: This is shown in the Micro-C contact maps in Figure 2B and C.

claim: DsRed is expressed throughout the posterior ~2/3rds of Fub-1 deletion embryos, with an anterior limit corresponding to the anterior border of PS6/A1.
source: Figure 3 shows that DsRed is expressed throughout the posterior ~2/3rds of Fub-1 deletion embryos, with an anterior limit corresponding to the anterior border of PS6/A1.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 by immunostaining of embryos.

claim: The reporter in DsRed-F1attP is insulated from the abx/bx domain, but is subject to regulation by the bxd/pbx domain.
source: Thus, as expected from the lack of phenotypic effects of the Fub-1 deletion, the reporter is insulated from the abx/bx domain, but is subject to regulation by the bxd/pbx domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern of DsRed shown in Figure 3.

claim: In DsRed-Fub-1 and Fub-1-GFP, the anterior border of expression of both DsRed and GFP corresponds to PS6/A1.
source: As shown in Figure 3, the anterior border of expression of both DsRed and GFP corresponds to the PS6/A1 as is observed for DsRed when the Fub-1 element is deleted.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 by immunostaining of embryos.

claim: Fub-1 is unable to block the bxd/pbx enhancers from activating the DsRed reporter in PS6/A1 cells.
source: Thus Fub-1 is unable to block the bxd/pbx enhancers from activating the DsRed reporter in PS6/A1 cells (and more posterior parasegments/segments), and this reporter is also 'located' within the bxd/pbx regulatory domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern of DsRed shown in Figure 3.

claim: An enhancer trap located 13 bp upstream of the Ubx transcription start site had a PS5/T3 anterior border, indicating that it is regulated by the abx/bx domain.
source: An enhancer trap located 13 bp upstream of the Ubx transcription start site had a PS5/T3 anterior border, indicating that it is regulated by the abx/bx domain.
evidence: This is based on previous enhancer trap studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: An enhancer trap located 196 bp upstream of the Ubx transcription start site had an anterior limit of expression shifted to PS6/A1.
source: In contrast, an enhancer trap located 196 bp upstream of the start site had an anterior limit of expression shifted to PS6/A1 (McCall et al., 1994).
evidence: This is based on previous enhancer trap studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The Ubx promoter region is sufficient for the functional autonomy of the abx/bx and bxd/pbx regulatory domains under laboratory growth conditions.
source: Taken together with the experiments described in the previous section, it would appear that the Ubx promoter region is sufficient for the functional autonomy of the abx/bx and bxd/pbx regulatory domains under laboratory growth conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the reporter expression data and the lack of phenotype in the Fub-1 deletion.

claim: Males carrying either the 1168 bp or the 753 bp Fub-1 replacements lack A6 just like the starting F7attP50 deletion.
source: Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 show that males carrying either the 1168 bp or the 753 bp replacements lack A6 just like the starting F7attP50 deletion.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 by adult cuticle preparations.

claim: The 1168 bp and 753 bp Fub-1 fragments do not prevent crosstalk between iab-6 and iab-7.
source: This result indicates that these two Fub-1 fragments do not prevent crosstalk between iab-6 and iab-7.
evidence: This is inferred from the GOF phenotype observed in the replacement flies.

claim: The HS1248-HS2505 replacement GOF phenotype is reflected in the pattern of Abd-B expression in the embryonic CNS that closely matches that of the starting F7attP50 deletion.
source: The HS1248-HS2505 replacement GOF phenotype is reflected in the pattern of Abd-B expression in the embryonic CNS that closely matches that of the starting F7attP50 deletion (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C by immunostaining of embryonic CNS.

claim: Both of the HS1 fragments (358 bp and 248 bp) block crosstalk between iab-6 and iab-7 and rescue the GOF transformation of A6 into A7.
source: Figure 4B shows that both of the HS1 fragments block crosstalk between iab-6 and iab-7 and rescue the GOF transformation of A6 into A7.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B by adult cuticle preparations.

claim: The rescuing activity of HS1 is orientation independent.
source: The rescuing activity is orientation independent.
evidence: This is shown by testing HS1 fragments in both forward and reverse orientations.

claim: In HS1 replacements, the morphology of the A6 segment resembles that normally observed in A5, not A6.
source: In all four cases, however, the morphology of the A6 segment resembles that normally observed in A5, not A6.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B by adult cuticle preparations.

claim: A mutation in the HS1 dCTCF binding site completely disrupts insulating activity.
source: Figure 4 shows that a mutation in the HS1 dCTCF binding site completely disrupts insulating activity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 by adult cuticle preparations and Abd-B staining.

claim: The adult HS1358mCTCF males lack the A6 segment, indicating that PS11/A6 is fully transformed into a copy of PS12/A7.
source: Like the starting F7attP50 platform, the adult HS1358mCTCF males lack the A6 segment, indicating that PS11/A6 is fully transformed into a copy of PS12/A7 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 by adult cuticle preparations.

claim: The pattern of Abd-B expression in HS1358mCTCF embryos is similar to that of F7attP50.
source: Consistent with a loss of blocking activity, the pattern of Abd-B expression in HS1358mCTCF embryos is similar to that of F7attP50 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C by immunostaining of embryonic CNS.

claim: An A6-like segment is present in HS2505R-SV40-HS1248R males.
source: Unlike the starting HS2505R-HS1248R line, an A6-like segment is present in HS2505R-SV40-HS1248R males (Figure 5B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 by adult cuticle preparations.

claim: Blocking is not fully restored to the level of HS1248R alone in HS2505R-SV40-HS1248R.
source: However, blocking is not fully restored to the level of HS1248R alone.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial rescue of the A6 segment morphology.

claim: In HS2505R-SV40-HS1248R males, the A6 tergite is slightly reduced in size while the sternite is absent.
source: In HS2505R-SV40-HS1248R males, the A6 tergite is slightly reduced in size while the sternite is absent.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B by adult cuticle preparations.

claim: In the embryonic CNS, Abd-B expression in PS11 is clearly elevated in HS2505R-SV40-HS1248R, but less so than that observed in either HS2505R-HS1248R or F7attP50.
source: In the embryonic CNS, Abd-B expression in PS11 is clearly elevated, but less so than that observed in either HS2505R-HS1248R or F7attP50 (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 by immunostaining of embryonic CNS.

claim: The insulating activity of HS2505R-mSV40-HS1248R is substantially compromised and only a residual A6 tergite is observed.
source: In contrast to HS2505R-SV40-HS1248R, the insulating activity of HS2505R-mSV40-HS1248R is substantially compromised and only a residual A6 tergite is observed (Figure 5B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 by adult cuticle preparations.

claim: HS2505R-HS1248R-SV40 has no boundary function: A6 is absent in males carrying the replacement.
source: Figures 5B and S4 and 4 show that just like HS2505R-HS1248R, HS2505R-HS1248R-SV40 has no boundary function: A6 is absent in males carrying the replacement, indicating that the cells in PS11/A6 have assumed a PS12/A7 identity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 by adult cuticle preparations.

claim: The Abd-B expression pattern in the embryonic CNS in HS2505R-HS1248R-SV40 closely matches that of HS2505R-HS1248R line.
source: The Abd-B expression pattern in the embryonic CNS also closely matches that of HS2505R-HS1248R line (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C by immunostaining of embryonic CNS.

claim: HS1 retains blocking activity in HS2505-HS1248R when HS2 is 'pointing' away from HS1.
source: Consistent with this prediction, HS1 retains blocking activity in HS2505-HS1248R.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and 5C by adult cuticle preparations and Abd-B staining.

claim: The pattern of Abd-B expression in the embryonic CNS in both PS10 and PS11 is reduced by HS2505-HS1248R.
source: Figure 5C shows that the pattern of Abd-B expression in the embryonic CNS in both PS10 and PS11 is reduced by HS2505-HS1248R, while the cuticle phenotype in adult males resembles HS1248 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C by immunostaining of embryonic CNS.

claim: Read-through transcription from HS2 is responsible for the inactivation of HS1 boundary function.
source: Taken together, these results show that read-through transcription from HS2 is responsible for the inactivation of HS1 boundary function.
evidence: This is inferred from the orientation-dependent effects and rescue by transcription terminators.

claim: The addition of four dCTCF sites (HS2505R-HS1248R-CTCFx4) is sufficient to rescue the blocking activity of HS1.
source: Figure 5B shows that the addition of four dCTCF sites (HS2505R-HS1248R-CTCFx4) is sufficient to rescue the blocking activity of HS1.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B by adult cuticle preparations.

claim: HS2505R-HS1248R-CTCFx4 males have a tergite and sternite whose morphology resembles that seen in A5.
source: As observed for HS1 alone, HS2505R-HS1248R-CTCFx4 males have a tergite and sternite whose morphology resembles that seen in A5.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B by adult cuticle preparations.

claim: The pattern of Abd-B expression in the CNS in HS2505R-HS1248R-CTCFx4 is similar to that observed for HS248.
source: Likewise, the pattern of Abd-B expression in the CNS in HS2505R-HS1248R-CTCFx4 is similar to that observed for HS248 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C by immunostaining of embryonic CNS.

claim: Fub-1HS2 sense transcripts were detected from PS6/A1 through PS12/A7 in WT embryos.
source: In WT embryos Fub-1HS2 sense (distal to proximal) transcripts were detected from PS6/A1 through PS12/A7.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B by smFISH.

claim: In Fub-1 deletion (F1attP) Fub-1HS2 transcripts were not detectable.
source: By contrast, in Fub-1 deletion (F1attP) Fub-1HS2 transcripts were not detectable.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B by smFISH.

claim: The intensity of the smFISH signal is higher in WT compared to F1attP at nuclear cycle 13.
source: Note that the intensity of the smFISH signal is higher in WT compared to F1attP.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 by smFISH.

claim: Both bxd and Fub-1HS2 lncRNAs are expressed at nuclear cycle 13 stage in WT embryos.
source: This finding indicates that both lncRNAs are expressed at this stage.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in smFISH signal intensity between WT and F1attP shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: At around stage 11 of embryogenesis, the transcription of bxd lncRNAs seems to be shut off as lncRNAs complementary to the probe are no longer detected in F1attP embryos.
source: At around stage 11 of embryogenesis, the transcription of bxd lncRNAs seems to be shut off as we no longer detect lncRNAs complementary to the probe in F1attP embryos (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3 by smFISH.

claim: At stage 11, only the Fub-1HS2 promoter seems to be active in WT embryos.
source: Thus, at this stage only the Fub-1HS2 promoter seems to be active.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of signal in F1attP but presence in WT at stage 11.

claim: Fub-1HS2 transcripts are detected in PS6/A1 through PS12/A7 at stage 11.
source: Like the DsRed and GFP reporters described above (Figure 3), Fub-1HS2 transcripts are detected in PS6/A1 through PS12/A7 (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3 by smFISH.

claim: In stage 14 embryos, Fub-1HS2 transcripts are detected in the epidermis in PS6–PS12, though the highest level is in PS6.
source: As shown in Figure 6B in stage 14 embryos, Fub-1HS2 transcripts are detected in the epidermis in PS6–PS12, though the highest level is in PS6.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B by smFISH.

claim: The pattern of Fub-1HS2 expression indicates that the HS2 promoter is regulated by the bxd/pbx domain, while it is insulated from regulatory elements in the abx/bx domain.
source: This pattern of expression indicates that the HS2 promoter is regulated by the bxd/pbx domain, while it is insulated from regulatory elements in the abx/bx domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the PS6/A1 anterior limit of Fub-1HS2 expression.

claim: The morphology of the A1 segment in HS2505R-HS1248R replacement flies is similar to that in WT.
source: As shown in Figure 6C, the morphology of the A1 segment in HS2505R-HS1248R replacement flies is similar to that in WT.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C by adult cuticle preparations.

claim: HS1248-HS2505R flies show evidence of an LOF transformation.
source: A different result is obtained for the replacement, HS1248-HS2505R, in which the HS2 promoter is directed away from HS1. HS1248-HS2505R flies show evidence of an LOF transformation (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C by adult cuticle preparations.

claim: HS1248-HS2505R transforms the first abdominal segment into the third thoracic: the first abdominal tergite is reduced or absent.
source: This replacement transforms the first abdominal segment into the third thoracic: the first abdominal tergite is reduced or absent; in addition, the posterior third thoracic segment is partly transformed to a posterior second thoracic segment: some flies have enlarged and/or pointing downward halters (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 4 by adult cuticle preparations.

claim: HS1248-HS2505R homozygotes display sterility.
source: HS1248-HS2505R homozygotes also display sterility.
evidence: This is an observed phenotype of the mutant flies.

claim: HS1248-HS2505R homozygous flies showed very low viability.
source: Homozygous flies showed very low viability, and we were able to generate homozygote larvae and flies only when growing heterozygotes on rich medium (Backhaus et al., 1984).
evidence: This is an observed phenotype of the mutant flies.

claim: In the HS1248-HS2505R replacement, the A1 band of denticles is narrower and irregular, indicative of an LOF transformation of A1 toward T3.
source: In the HS1248-HS2505R replacement, the A1 band of denticles is narrower and irregular, indicative of an LOF transformation of A1 toward T3 (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5 by larval cuticle preparations.

claim: A reduction in the expression of Ubx in the posterior compartment of the haltere discs is observed in HS1248-HS2505R compared to WT.
source: We also observe a reduction in the expression of Ubx in the posterior compartment of the haltere discs compared to WT (Figure 6—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 6 by immunostaining of imaginal discs.

claim: Antisense transcripts complementary to the smFISH probes are not detected in WT embryos.
source: Figure 7 shows that as expected antisense transcripts complementary to the smFISH probes are not detected in WT embryos.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 by smFISH.

claim: Segmentally restricted antisense transcripts are expressed in both HS1248-HS2505R and HS2505R-HS1248R.
source: In contrast, segmentally restricted antisense transcripts are expressed in both of the Fub-1 replacements.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 by smFISH.

claim: The antisense transcripts are detected in PS6/A1 through PS12/A7 in HS1248-HS2505R and HS2505R-HS1248R.
source: Like Fub-1HS2 sense transcripts in WT (Figure 6), the antisense transcripts are detected in PS6/A1 through PS12/A7 in HS1248-HS2505R and HS2505R-HS1248R.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 by smFISH.

claim: The antisense transcript signal is noticeably greater in HS1248-HS2505R than it is in HS2505R-HS1248R.
source: The transcripts levels in HS1248-HS2505R and HS2505R-HS1248R embryos are not, however, equivalent. The signal is noticeably greater in HS1248-HS2505R than it is in HS2505R-HS1248R.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 by smFISH.

claim: Sense transcription is not detectable in HS1248-HS2505R when HS2 is inverted.
source: Figure 7 shows that, unlike WT (Figure 6), sense transcription is not detectable when HS2 is inverted.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 by smFISH.

claim: The lncRNA promoter is situated in HS2 and drives transcription only in one direction.
source: This result indicates that the lncRNA promoter is situated in HS2 and drives transcription only in one direction.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of sense transcripts when HS2 is inverted.

claim: HS1 is a dCTCF-dependent boundary element.
source: We show here that HS1 is a dCTCF-dependent boundary element, while HS2 is a developmentally regulated promoter that directs transcription through HS1 inactivating its boundary function in parasegments that require Ubx function.
evidence: This is supported by the requirement for dCTCF binding sites for HS1 blocking activity.

claim: HS2 is a developmentally regulated promoter that directs transcription through HS1 inactivating its boundary function in parasegments that require Ubx function.
source: We show here that HS1 is a dCTCF-dependent boundary element, while HS2 is a developmentally regulated promoter that directs transcription through HS1 inactivating its boundary function in parasegments that require Ubx function.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claim: All but three of the BX-C regulatory domains must be able to bypass one or more intervening boundary elements to direct the proper expression of their target homeotic gene.
source: However, in order to direct the proper expression of their target homeotic gene, all but three of the regulatory domains must be able to bypass one or more intervening boundary elements.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BX-C regulatory architecture.

claim: The three homeotic genes and their associated regulatory domains are arranged so that all but three of the domains are separated from their targets by one or more intervening boundaries.
source: The three homeotic genes and their associated regulatory domains are arranged so that all but three of the domains are separated from their targets by one or more intervening boundaries.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BX-C genomic organization.

claim: Fab-7 has bypass activity and it mediates regulatory interactions between iab-6 and Abd-B.
source: For example, Fab-7 has bypass activity and it mediates regulatory interactions between iab-6 and Abd-B.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Fab-7 function, supported by citations.

claim: When Fab-7 is replaced by generic fly boundaries (e.g., scs or su(Hw)) or by BX-C boundaries that lack bypass activity (Mcp), these boundaries block crosstalk but do not support bypass.
source: However, when Fab-7 is replaced by generic fly boundaries (e.g., scs or su(Hw)) or by BX-C boundaries that lack bypass activity (Mcp), these boundaries block crosstalk but do not support bypass (Hogga et al., 2001; Kyrchanova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: When Fab-7 is replaced by boundaries that lack bypass activity, Abd-B expression in PS11/A6 is driven by iab-5 not iab-6, resulting in a loss-of-function (LOF) phenotype.
source: As a consequence, Abd-B expression in PS11/A6 is driven by iab-5 not iab-6, and this results in a loss-of-function (LOF) phenotype.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the consequences of replacing Fab-7 with non-bypass boundaries.

claim: The Ubx domain is delimited and subdivided by three boundaries called Fub-2, Fub-1, and Fub.
source: The Ubx domain is delimited and subdivided by three boundaries called Fub-2, Fub-1, and Fub.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ubx regulatory architecture, supported by citations.

claim: Fub-2 and Fub-1 flank abx/bx domain, whereas bxd/pbx is flanked by Fub-1 and Fub.
source: Fub-2 and Fub-1 flank abx/bx domain, whereas bxd/pbx is flanked by Fub-1 and Fub (Figure 1; Bowman et al., 2014; Mateo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and supported by citations.

claim: Fub-1 would have to be bypassed so that bxd/pbx can direct Ubx expression in PS6/A1.
source: As Fub-1 separates enhancers in bxd/pbx regulatory domain from Ubx gene (Figure 1), it would have to be bypassed so that bxd/pbx can direct Ubx expression in PS6/A1.
evidence: This is inferred from the genomic organization shown in Figure 1.

claim: Segmentally regulated transcription of an lncRNA disrupts the blocking activity of Fub-1, enabling enhancers in the bxd/pbx regulatory domain to activate Ubx in PS6/A1 cells.
source: Here we show that segmentally regulated transcription of an lncRNA disrupts the blocking activity of Fub-1, enabling enhancers in the bxd/pbx regulatory domain to activate Ubx in PS6/A1 cells.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.
